extracted.intended_audience: parties (claimants and respondents), their counsel, and other participants in Copyright Claims Board (CCB) proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative standards governing discovery, evidence, hearings, deadlines, and smaller-claims procedures before the Copyright Claims Board, including formatting and submission requirements for eCCB filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for Admission (RFAs) — limited, for good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for admission are classified as a form of additional discovery that the CCB may allow 'on a limited basis' and 'for good cause shown.' They will not be available as 'of right,' and requesting parties must provide the specific RFAs they seek to propound and show good cause for each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction is intended to streamline discovery and address concerns that RFAs encourage 'semantic battles' and would be burdensome for pro se litigants; it aligns with commenters who supported limited use. Parties seeking RFAs must specify each request and justify why good cause exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production of Documents — scope and tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Document production obligations are narrowed to avoid overbroad requests; e.g., for financial information the Office agreed with limiting production to documents that are not unduly burdensome and revised phrasing to require documents 'sufficient to show' certain matters and in some contexts 'documents directly pertaining to' the matter (e.g., truth or falsity of representations). The broad category '[a]ll documents related to damages' was removed and other categories were narrowed by adding 'in the proceeding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rules aim to balance relevance with burden: discovery requests should be tailored and not encompass large volumes of irrelevant materials. Where relevant, licensing history may be discoverable. For misrepresentation claims, production is limited to documents directly pertaining to truth or falsity to avoid overbroad discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege and Withholding of Documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential communications between a party and its counsel reflecting or seeking legal advice related to the merits of the proceeding are categorically privileged and need not be produced. Parties seeking to withhold other types of documents must first seek and receive leave of the CCB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office declined to insert broad legal terminology that might confuse pro se parties but explicitly preserves attorney-client privilege for communications about merits. For other asserted privileges or protections, leave of the Board is required before withholding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Search for Responsive Documents and ESI
rubrics_metrics.description: A party's obligation to search for responsive documents is limited to files in the party's possession or under their control, and to files of any agents, employees, representatives, or others acting on the party's behalf 'who the party reasonably believes may have responsive documents.' If a party reasonably believes that responsive documents are in its possession or control, including emails and computer files, it must conduct a reasonable search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office rejects categorical prohibitions on custodial email searches; the standard is reasonableness. The rule establishes an explicit reasonable investigation standard for discovery responses. Manual baseline searches 'need not,' rather than 'shall not,' be exceeded — parties may run more extensive searches where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluminous Productions ('document dumps') and Bad-Faith Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Document productions that include large amounts of irrelevant or duplicative material ('document dumps') are not automatically per se bad faith; such voluminous productions 'may,' rather than 'shall,' constitute bad-faith conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CCB retains discretion to assess bad faith 'in light of all relevant context' rather than treating voluminous production as automatically bad faith; determinations will consider the surrounding circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions Prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions will not be permitted in CCB proceedings. Testimony is primarily submitted in written form and oral testimony is presented only at a hearing conducted before the CCB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule explicitly bars depositions to streamline proceedings and reduce burdens on parties, particularly pro se participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert Witnesses Highly Disfavored
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of expert witnesses in proceedings before the Board is highly disfavored and requests shall be rarely granted. The CCB will grant a request 'only in exceptional circumstances and upon a showing that the case cannot fairly proceed without the use of the expert.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because typical damages caps and costs make experts impractical, parties are not required to disclose intent to use experts at the outset. Requests to present experts should demonstrate why the case cannot fairly proceed without expert testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Testimony — accommodations and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office will provide guidance (in the CCB Handbook) on drafting written testimony. Parties are provided 15 additional days to file response testimony (45 total) and 7 additional days to file reply testimony (21 total). Certain procedural burdens (e.g., witness sponsorship of documentary evidence) are omitted to make submission easier; the Office will create forms to simplify submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules are tailored to be accessible to pro se parties: extended filing windows, streamlined authentication practices, and forms aim to reduce legalese and procedural complexity. Handbook will include specific drafting topics requested by commenters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearings — virtual format, informality, and Officer/Attorney roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings are virtual except as expressly described in statute; the CCB will not mirror Federal courtroom practices. Questioning during hearings will be significantly less formal and regimented; Parties may ask questions of witnesses, but formal objections to evidence are eliminated. Copyright Claims Officers shall determine claims and defenses, rule on scheduling, discovery, evidentiary, and other matters, conduct hearings and conferences, and make damage awards. Copyright Claims Attorneys may assist Officers and provide administrative or procedural assistance to parties, but substantive disputes are referred to Officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office envisions Officers taking an active role in managing hearings, guiding pro se participants, and asking their own questions of witnesses to fully develop testimony. Exhibits not submitted in written testimony may not be used at a hearing without leave of the CCB. In-person hearings are generally not provided for except as statute permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibits and Use of Evidence at Hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibits not submitted in written testimony may not be used at a hearing without leave of the CCB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To streamline procedures and accommodate parties unfamiliar with formal rules of evidence, the final rule more directly bars use of exhibits not previously submitted in written testimony unless the Board grants leave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Determination Review and Reconsideration Procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute provides two levels of review: reconsideration by the CCB and review by the Register of Copyrights. The party opposing an initial reconsideration may request reconsideration or amendment of the amended final determination; if unsuccessful before the CCB, that party may then request review by the Register. The filing fee for Register review is $300.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office adopted procedures to avoid unfairness where an initially prevailing party loses on reconsideration by permitting that party to seek reconsideration/amendment and then, if unsuccessful, Register review. The $300 fee is maintained to discourage prolonging proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data Collection and Reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The CCB will track data relevant to its operations internally and will ultimately issue a public report on the CCB that will likely include case statistics (e.g., number of cases filed, defaulting respondents, opt-outs, waivers of service, how often defaults are corrected, and types/amounts of damages awards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data collection is intended to be transparent and anonymized and to inform fair procedures and identify potential abuses of the process; the Office aligns this with its Strategic Plan goal to enhance data as an evidentiary foundation for policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaller Claims — definition and streamlined procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller claims are those in which total damages sought do not exceed $5,000. Smaller claims are determined by at least one Officer and follow a streamlined process: discovery is significantly limited (typically to what is appended to the claim/response unless additional narrowly tailored discovery is approved), expert testimony is not permitted, and hearings are not permitted. The process uses written submissions, an initial conference, a party position statement, a merits conference, tentative findings of fact by the presiding Officer with an opportunity for parties to respond, and a final determination. Counterclaims for damages above the smaller-claims limit are not permitted. A claimant may change its election between smaller and standard proceedings before service of the initial notice; smaller-claims notices must indicate the claim is a smaller claim and briefly explain procedural differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presiding Officer will ensure any approved discovery is narrowly tailored, unlikely to impose undue burden, and highly likely to yield relevant evidence. Only written statements (no responsive statements) and no expert testimony are allowed; the Officer may question witnesses at the merits conference. These procedures are intended to make smaller claims faster, less formal, and less burdensome for claimants and respondents, particularly to encourage participation rather than opting out.

rubrics_metrics.name: eCCB Submission Tiers, Character Limits, and Response Deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless otherwise provided or ordered, many requests and responses must be submitted through a fillable form on eCCB and comply with tiered character limits and response windows: Tier one submissions are limited to 4,000 characters with responses permitted within 7 days; Tier two submissions are limited to 10,000 characters (attachments excluded) with responses permitted within 14 days. The Board may deny a request before the time to respond expires but will not grant a request before the response period expires unless all parties consent. Replies by a party who submits a request are not allowed absent leave of the Board. Specified categories of motions and requests are enumerated for each tier (e.g., scheduling amendments, requests for hearings in tier one; requests to amend pleadings, consolidate, intervene, additional discovery, requests to serve RFAs, and to present expert witnesses in tier two).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must use the designated tiers for particular request types and adhere to character limits and response deadlines. For requests for additional discovery, the specific discovery requests (e.g., individual interrogatories, document requests, RFAs) must be entered within the fillable form. The procedural rule prevents premature grants and limits back-and-forth replies unless the Board allows them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and Filing Rules for Deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: When the start or end date for calculating any deadline falls on a weekend or a Federal holiday, the start or end date is extended to the next Federal workday. Any document subject to a deadline must be either submitted to the Board's electronic filing system (eCCB) by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on the date of the deadline or dispatched by the date of the deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict adherence to time rules is required; electronic filing by 11:59 p.m. ET on the deadline date satisfies filing requirements, otherwise physical dispatch by that date is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad-Faith Conduct — general definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad-faith conduct occurs when a party pursues a claim, counterclaim, or defense for a harassing or other improper purpose, or without a reasonable basis in law or fact. Such conduct includes any actions taken in support of a claim, counterclaim, or defense and may occur at any point during a proceeding before the Board, including before a proceeding becomes an active proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad definition permits the Board to sanction or act against conduct intended to harass or otherwise abuse the process. Assessments of bad faith will consider context and are not limited to a single stage of the proceeding.
